#3277. Why I'd Choose the Oura Ring 5 Over the Cheaper Ultrahuman Pro

Ultrahuman’s Ring Pro is now officially on sale in the U.S., which makes this the perfect time to consider how this new device compares to the reigning champ in the smart ring market, the Oura Ring 5. Here's the short answer: While there’s a lot to like in the Ultrahuman Ring Pro, ultimately I think the Oura Ring 5 is just better at doing its job.

I’ve spent plenty of time with both rings, and admittedly, many of the differences between the two will come down to personal preference—for example, do you like the biohacking concept and the “next best actions” suggestions in the Ultrahuman app, or do you favor the soothing vibes of the Oura app? But when it comes to the devices themselves, there are big differences between them in terms of size, cost, and overall ease of use. Here’s my take on each, and why Oura is still my top choice.

The Oura Ring 5 is impressively small, and when you have to wear something on your finger, size matters a lot—and generally, smaller is better. The Oura Ring 5 is the smallest and most comfortable smart ring I’ve ever worn. I have a ton of photos here comparing it in size to other smart rings (including RingConn, older Oura rings, and an older Ultrahuman); suffice it to say, the Oura Ring 5 wins this category easily.

When it comes to the interior fit, both rings are similar: mostly smooth on the inside, without any intrusive bumps. But considering the overall shape and feel, the Oura Ring 5 is just more comfortable to wear throughout an entire day.

The Oura Ring 5 comes with a plug-in charger, which isn’t very convenient, but will get the job done. You can buy a slim, rounded charging case that easily fits in your pocket for $99. You need to match the size of the case to the size of your ring, and the charging case is not compatible with earlier versions of the device. It’s good for 30 days of charge, according to Oura.

The Ultrahuman Ring Pro comes with a charging case that is heavy and bulky with prominent corners, but good for an extra 45 days of battery life. The case fits any size of Ultrahuman Ring Pro, but is not compatible with previous versions. You can have the case play sounds if you’ve misplaced it.

The Ultrahuman ring lasts slightly longer on a charge: eight to 10 days, according to the company, versus six to nine for the Oura Ring 5. The Ultrahuman ring also has several different battery modes, with “chill mode” lasting me about two weeks.

To sum up: the Ultrahuman ring lasts longer on a charge and has more capacity in its charging case. You also get the charging case for free. But the Oura Ring 5’s charging case is smaller and much easier to carry around. Once again, we’re looking at two decent options: The Oura case is more expensive for what you get, but it’s also nicer to use.

Oura is the most expensive smart ring out there, and it requires a subscription. That makes it the priciest option, giving Ultrahuman an opening to beat it simply by virtue of being cheaper. But this one is closer to a wash, depending on the choices you make. If you’re looking for the cheapest possible smart ring, well, you’d probably end up with something else entirely, like a RingConn Air. But between the Oura Ring 5 and the Ultrahuman Ring Pro, the latter is cheaper than the Oura Ring 5...but only if you’re saying no to all the extras. Let me break it down.

The Oura Ring 5 costs $399 for the shiny black and silver models, and $499 for gold, rose, and the matte versions of the black and silver. The subscription costs $5.99/month (or $69.99/year, which is only a $2 savings), and the Oura is basically useless without the subscription.

Here's how the cost works out on an annual basis:

Oura Ring 5 in black or silver: $399 + $5.99/month subscription = $470.88 for one year, $542.76 for two years

Oura Ring 5 in other colors: $499 + $5.99/month subscription = $570.88 for one year, $642.76 for two years.

The Ultrahuman Ring Pro is $479 for all colors, and there is no subscription for basic use of the ring. But you can't necessarily stop there, because the Ultrahuman app includes “PowerPlugs” that will give you extra features or analysis screens. Some are totally free, including the caffeine window,  smart alarms, a new parent mode, and a limited version of the cycle and ovulation tracker, but others carry a monthly fee. And if you consider all the optional subscription fees for different PowerPlugs, they can quickly add up:

HealthEx, to connect medical records: $4.99/month

Most people probably wouldn't choose all of them, but even if you just wanted, say, respiratory health and cycle & ovulation pro, you’d quickly outstrip the price of an Oura Ring’s subscription. On the other hand, Ultrahuman also offers an Ultrahuman Max plan for $9.99/month or $99.99/year that includes all the PowerPlugs mentioned above, plus the Les Mills workouts that normally run $11.99/month. That's cheaper than subscribing to all of the options individually, but it will also make the Ultrahuman Ring Pro more expensive than the Oura Ring 5: $578.99 total for one year, or $678.98 for two years. In short, if you want everything that each ring has to offer, the Ultrahuman will cost you more.

Here's the big caveat: I wouldn't recommend bothering with most of the PowerPlugs. For example, "UltraSync for Tesla" recommends settings for your car based on how rested you are, which will be useless if you don't have a Tesla, and probably even if you do. "Cardio adaptability" measures a metric that Ultrahuman says is subtly different from HRV; Oura doesn't measure this adaptability metric, but it's not clear to me whether it's even worth measuring at all (I'd argue probably not).

Ultrahuman's respiratory health PowerPlug ($3.99/month) records sounds while you sleep, which Oura doesn't do; but Oura reports breathing disturbances based on the ring's data, which Ultrahuman doesn't do. Ultrahuman's feature is more expensive.

Ultrahuman offers a premium version of its cycle tracker for $3.99/month, while Oura has a partnership with Natural Cycles that cost $149.99/year. Either will provide more detailed (and, each company says, more accurate) cycle tracking than the basic tracking each app provides without the extras. Oura's option is more expensive.

Ultrahuman's HealthEx Powerplug ($4.99/month) displays information from your medical records throughout the app; Oura lets you import your medical records for free, but uses them mainly in the Advisor (chatbot) and dedicated areas of the app. Ultrahuman's option is more expensive.

Oura's app gives you scores for your readiness, sleep, and recent activity, and it tracks how stressed you seem to be throughout the day. A message at the top of the main screen gives you advice for what to do that day—for example, scaling back your workouts if you seem to be tired or stressed. Ultrahuman does pretty much the same thing, giving you a "next best action" that changes throughout the day, but tends to stick to predictable themes: get more activity if you've been sitting, and that sort of thing.

Both give detailed breakdowns of the factors that contribute to your scores, and both likely overstate how useful their scores are (you don't actually need to change your workout plans just because you had a less-than-perfect night of sleep). But the apps handle the basics pretty similarly: Both have partners and integrations, and you can book blood tests through either app, if you want to do that for some reason.

Ultrahuman gives you a bit more guidance on circadian rhythms, urging you to get in extra steps during certain times of day, and offering to micromanage your caffeine intake. It has a "longevity" tab that puts your long-term habits in terms of how many years they are supposedly subtracting from (or adding to) your lifespan, including measurable metrics like VO2max and a few things that are more inscrutable, like arterial stiffness.

Oura has a whole tab of "vitals" that it calculates from your day-to-day data, which I find more useful than Ultrahuman's data views. The items here include "resilience," which compares your stress to your recovery; a "symptom radar" that can sometimes flag when you're sick; and metrics of sleep regularity and how you're breathing. And, of course, you can check your "cardiovascular age" to see how much younger (or older) you should feel.

Overall, I prefer Oura's approach because the metrics make more sense, are easier to find, and are less likely to feel like they're going way out on a limb relative to the underlying science. Ultrahuman wants you to feel like a cutting-edge biohacker; Oura does a bit more to keep things down to earth. It is a bit funny to remember that both apps, and their wealth of data, are basically just pulling from heart rate readings throughout the day and night. Neither app gives you any truly important information the other doesn't, but Oura's makes more sense to me.

#3275. This Hidden Device Could Free Up Gigawatts of Grid Power

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

Variable frequency drives can slash motors’ power use

Zurich-based ABB is one of several manufacturers of variable frequency drives (VFDs), such as this ACH580. VFDs could help make the millions of electric motors running in industrial facilities more energy efficient.

This article was originally published by Canary Media.

America’s energy supply crunch is driving a surge of federal and private investment in new electricity generation—from polluting gas turbines to cleaner developments like solar farms and geothermal plants. But gigawatts of power are already available for the taking across the U.S. economy in the form of wasted energy from an unexpected source: motors.

Some 50 million electric motors drive the fans, pumps, and compressors found in virtually every factory and building. Together, they gobble enough electricity to equal nearly a third of total U.S. power demand. Often, the motors use far more energy than they actually need to keep America’s machines humming.

Companies can install devices known as variable frequency drives, or VFDs, to make motors run super efficiently. Yet adoption remains relatively low, in part because of the perceived hassle of retrofitting equipment and because they’re typically not required. On average, only 16 percent of motor systems at industrial facilities and 4 percent of commercial-sector motors use VFDs, according to a 2021 market report by Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory.

However, there are now more reasons than ever to equip the nation’s motors with power-saving devices, energy experts and device manufacturers say. They’re urging federal agencies, utilities, and deep-pocketed tech giants to spur a wider rollout of VFDs through financial incentives and efficiency standards.

For one, slashing motors’ power use would free up grid capacity for large electricity users like data centers and electric vehicles, they argue. It would help curb costs for factories that are switching from fossil-fueled heating systems to electrified, motor-based solutions like heat pumps—all at a time when industrial power prices are climbing fast. Plus, VFD technology has become far more sophisticated and less expensive to install than earlier iterations.

“This is low-hanging fruit that gives a lot [of energy] back and is reasonably simple,” Nik Sawe, a senior policy analyst at the nonpartisan think tank Energy Innovation, says of the technology.

Energy-wise, the main problem with electric motors is that they’re always running at full capacity. Consider an office building, which empties out in the evening. The heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning system can wind down in those hours, with dampers and valves restricting the flow of cold or hot air. But the motors and fans that drive the whole setup are still working in the background, wasting energy.

VFD technology, such as the Danfoss iC7 series, has gained some momentum in recent years among factories and buildings trying to combat rising electricity costs. Danfoss Drives

VFDs are electronic controllers with temperature sensors that continually adjust the speed of motors, automatically ramping up or down to match demand. The technology, which is also called adjustable speed drives, has the potential to curb a motor’s energy use by around 40 to 60 percent, says Neal Elliott, director emeritus of the American Council for an Energy-Efficient Economy.

All those energy reductions add up. Toyota, for example, installed VFDs on over 200 motors inside the HVAC system at its auto manufacturing plant in Georgetown, Kentucky, as part of a US $1.25 million pilot project in 2015. The automaker saved more than $700,000 in annual electricity costs thanks to the VFDs, and it continues to use the technology at other manufacturing facilities across the U.S., the company said by email.

“We’ve known for many, many years that there’s a huge opportunity for energy savings by varying the speed of the motor,” says Elliott, who noted that he literally wrote the book on energy-efficient motor systems in 2002.

Certain aspects of the technology have historically held the drives back since they debuted in the late 1960s. Measuring the flow of water, air, refrigerant—whatever is moving through the system that the motors are driving—was for decades an expensive engineering process. Accurately controlling motors to deliver the right amount of juice, at just the right time, faced similar issues.

But recent advances in sensors and machine-learning algorithms have significantly slashed the cost and complexity of using drives, Elliott says. Modern VFDs have also benefited from the increased production of advanced power chips that are used in high-voltage applications such as electric vehicles and solar power inverters.

Another long-standing challenge has been that commercial and industrial building developers often prioritize reducing upfront costs over netting long-term energy savings, and so they don’t always build to the highest efficiency levels, says Zack Valdez, senior director of regulatory and industry affairs at the National Electrical Manufacturers Association, whose members include drive and motor makers.

“If the facility that you’re putting it into doesn’t require it, then oftentimes people will overlook [VFDs], because they’re just trying to build to a minimum set of energy requirements,” he says. And if companies don’t install drives from the start, they’re likely less inclined to take time to retrofit an operating system.

The trade association recently launched a pilot program with manufacturers, utilities, and energy-efficiency groups to collect real-world data about how VFDs reduce motors’ electricity use and lower utility bills. The goal is to demonstrate how the technology can benefit not only individual facilities but also the wider grid—giving utilities a concrete reason to provide rebates for industrial customers.

Proponents say they hope the results will help the U.S. Department of Energy shape future efficiency measures and incentives that encourage adoption of the drives, including in federally owned buildings. Despite the Trump administration’s open hostility toward home appliance and equipment mandates, agency staff have apparently been receptive to discussing solutions that could meet the soaring power needs of data centers.

“If you added a drive to all the motors that are out there, you could provide [power for] up to five years of data center growth without having to build any new generation,” says Kirk Anderson, director of government relations and public affairs for ABB. The global manufacturing giant makes VFDs domestically near Milwaukee.

Anderson floated the idea of having tech companies help pay for factory owners to install VFDs to free up room on the grid. After all, hyperscalers are already spending many billions of dollars to revive shuttered nuclear plants, support next-generation geothermal projects, deploy fleets of grid-scale batteries, and supercharge the build-out of gas turbines and power plants.

“Instead of ‘bring your own power,’ it should be ‘offset your own power,’” he says, referring to a growing effort by states to get data centers to secure their own power resources and prevent rising costs for regular customers.

Michael Reckamp, the director of enterprise strategy for Danfoss Drives, North America, another VFD manufacturer, said that despite the traditionally low adoption rates, the technology has gained some momentum in recent years among factories and buildings as rising electricity costs and other grid-wide challenges make it harder to justify wasting energy.

Still, “it hasn’t permeated enough to get everyone utilizing it,” he says. “In the current situation, where we’re having so many issues with grids, brownouts, and now data centers wanting to take the load, I think there should be a renewed focus on putting drives out there to really reduce the stress on the grid and improve energy savings.”

Maria Gallucci is a clean-energy reporter with Canary Media.

The game is back on for AMD vs Intel handheld gaming

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

AMD finally dropped FSR 4 for integrated silicon — officially bringing next-generation upscaling to the Z Extreme handhelds and Strix Halo laptops. It’s built to be AMD’s silver bullet against Nvidia’s DLSS. A massive, free software upgrade that magically boosts picture quality and hands you more frames per second.

So over the past week, I’ve updated my ROG Xbox Ally X20 and TUF Gaming A14 with the new drivers and fired up the benchmarking tools to see what AMD has cooked.

And what I found completely breaks the current narrative. We’re all trained to think a new version of AI game scaling tech will send your frame rates skyrocketing. If you come in with that assumption, you’ll be left disappointed.

However, if you understand the optical illusion AMD has actually pulled off here (and how Performance mode is now the new Balanced), it completely changes how you will game on Team Red’s silicon.

If you have a compatible AMD handheld or APU, they have thankfully baked this early-access driver directly into their software. Here is how to activate it on the ROG Xbox Ally X20:

Open Armory Crate and navigate to the Update Center. Go to the Preview Updates tab and install the new AMD Radeon graphics driver (dated October 23 or newer).

Once restarted, press the Armory Crate button to open the side Command Center, hit the Edit icon, and add the new AMD FSR Upscaling tile. Activate it.

You cannot toggle this on the fly mid-game. You must turn the FSR upscaling tile on in the Command Center before you launch your game, and then select the FSR setting inside the game's display menus.

As for with Strix Halo laptops, you just need the latest AMD Adrenalin drivers to get it, so get those updated!

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

So let’s get into the actual numbers. My standard FSR advice has always been to leave it on the Balanced preset. But when I ran one-to-one tests comparing FSR 3 against the new FSR 4 on the exact same settings, the new tech didn’t give me more frames.

2560 x 1600 high FSR Balanced (Frame gen)

So why is it slower? FSR 4 isn’t just a simple spatial algorithm anymore. It's a heavier, vastly more complex machine-learning model — requiring more overhead and compute power to analyze and reconstruct the image.

A direct preset-to-preset comparison doesn’t math. You have to change the way you use it.

Through my testing, one thing became abundantly clear: FSR 4 running in Performance actually delivers a notable picture quality increase over FSR 3 running in Balanced mode.

This is the true breakthrough. With FSR 3, dropping your game down to Performance meant accepting a blurry, pixelated picture — especially in motion. FSR 4 is so much sharper at rebuilding images that it’s not a compromise anymore.

In Dying Light: The Beast, you can see that foliage and stonework come through with much more clarity with FSR 4 vs FSR 3. At that lower internal resolution, AMD’s able to pick up and upscale more detail.

In Spider-Man: Miles Morales, it becomes so clear when you look at the fur detailing on the jacket collar. With FSR 3, it’s softer and clumpier, whereas individual hairs are more sharply defined with the 4th generation.

Moving over to Cyberpunk 2077, that NPC is rendered much more sharply — especially in the hair. Forza Horizon 6 shows a sharpening of the reflections on that wet asphalt, and there’s cleaner edges to details like computer screens and the robotic suit in Pragmata.

All of this on performance, and the numbers take a jump too.

2560 x 1600 high FSR Balanced (Frame gen)

FSR 4 is the biggest free upgrade AMD handhelds and laptops have received in a long time, but only if you rewire how you tweak your settings.

Make no mistake about it. FSR 4 is the biggest free upgrade AMD handhelds and laptops have received in a long time, but only if you rewire how you tweak your settings. It’s not a one-to-one swap for a Balanced preset — a confident drop to Performance mode will get you a better picture quality and frame rate to boost.

But after the past few months of watching Intel really take the gaming fight to AMD with Panther Lake chips and XeSS 3, is this enough to take on Team Blue? Sort of.

This is a catch up effort, but there are places where Intel continues to lead, such as with a stronger GPU silicon on handhelds and multi-frame generation. But that Arc G3 Extreme is definitely pricier.

It’ll be interesting to see how this all plays out! And if you've noticed differences in your own experiences, let me know in the comments box below.

#3273. iOS 27.3 adds all-new Apple Health app, details here

Apple released iOS 27.3 beta 1 today, and it reintroduces the all-new Health app that was first available for testing during the iOS 27.2 beta. Here’s what’s new.

iOS 27.3 will launch with an upgraded Apple Health app. The new app was initially tested during the iOS 27.2 beta, but it’s back today in iOS 27.3 beta 1 and will ship to all users next month.

Today on Apple Newsroom, the company outlined what to expect from the new Health experience.

Three central new Health features are highlighted for iOS 27.3:

Insights tab: “surfaces timely, holistic summaries spanning heart, sleep, readiness, fitness, vitals, and cycle tracking data throughout the day. A dedicated For You section delivers intelligent recommendations tailored to a user’s daily habits — such as practical guidance to adjust a wind-down routine following consecutive nights of interrupted sleep. The app pairs data with dynamic health content, offering educational videos and articles featuring Health app clinical experts.”

Longevity tab: “analyzes longitudinal metrics across heart health, sleep, mental wellbeing, movement, metabolic health, hearing, and nutrition. Central to this tab is Health Age, a feature that translates data from Apple Watch — including VO2 max, resting heart rate, sleep, and heart rate variability — into a metric that reflects how a user’s body is tracking relative to their chronological age. Users can also incorporate clinical laboratory data, such as A1c and LDL cholesterol, to enrich their long-term health picture.”

At-home movement evaluations: “make physical assessments accessible without requiring specialized equipment. Using an iPhone camera and Apple Watch, users can measure their flexibility, strength, balance, movement mechanics, and VO2 max with real-time audio and visual feedback. Powered by on-device vision-based AI models and developed with clinical experts, the experience runs entirely on device; no video is ever recorded, stored, or shared.“

Additionally, Apple says that the new Health app offers expanded language support. It is available in global English, Chinese (Simplified and Traditional), French, Japanese, Korean, Norwegian, Portuguese, Spanish, Turkish, and Vietnamese.

What do you think of the new Health app in iOS 27.3? Let us know in the comments.

#3272. Five Creative Ways to Spend Your FSA Funds Before the End of the Year

If you have a flexible spending account (FSA), you know the drill: Use the funds before the end of the year, or lose them. Unfortunately, chances are slim you can pack the rest of the year with doctor's appointments. Does that mean your hard-earned funds go to waste? Definitely not. You can spend your remaining FSA funds on other qualifying healthcare costs. And what counts as "qualifying" might surprise you—for instance, you can use your FSA or HSA funds to get yourself a sweet new fitness tracker or smartwatch.

As the end of the year approaches, here are all the ways you can spend any leftover money in your FSA balance.

Many over-the-counter medications and health items are FSA-eligible, including pain relievers, cold medicine, bandages, dental care products, menstrual products, and more. Scan your medicine cabinet and make a list of anything you need to stock up on.

FSA/HSA eligibility for smartwatches and other fitness wearables is real, but the main “catch" (as I’ve previously explained) is proving the device is in fact necessary, which requires you to obtain a Letter of Medical Necessity (LMN).

Screenless recovery trackers like Whoop, Amazfit Helio Strap, and the Oura Ring can usually be justified as HSA/FSA eligible around sleep quality, HRV-based stress monitoring, or recovery tracking tied to a chronic condition. Similarly, smartwatches can qualify the same way a basic tracker does, as long as you can link a relevant documented health concern. For instance, Coros offers FSA/HSA eligibility for all its watches and heart rate monitors through its partnership with Truemed. Amazfit similarly lets you filter by HSA/FSA eligibility for its smartwatches.

If you want to get creative with it, the official FSA store lets you filter by "surprisingly eligible." Similar to the section above, for some of these items, you'll want to brush up on how exactly to get an LMN to justify certain tech as FSA-eligible for you personally. In the meantime, go crazy and snag yourself Epsom salt for $8.99, Supergoop! sunscreen for $38.00, or perhaps a snazzy massage gun for $349.99.

Knee braces, wrist splints, compression socks, and other orthopedic items can help relieve chronic pain issues. Rather than wait for these issues to rear their heads down the line, use FSA money to offset the costs of these fixes now. If you use eyeglasses or contacts, consider using your FSA dollars to update or refresh your prescriptions. Don't forget to stock up on eye drops and lens solution, too.

If you have medical procedures scheduled for early next year, many healthcare providers will allow you to pre-pay the estimated costs this calendar year using FSA funds. This includes dental work, physical therapy, chiropractic visits, Lasik eye surgery, and more.

However you choose to spend your FSA funds, don’t let that money go to waste. After all, it came out of your paycheck. Check in with your employer’s rules for any balance remaining on Dec. 31 this year, so you aren’t left forfeiting your hard-earned funds. You can find a complete list at the FSA store here.

#3270. Xavier Becerra Elected California Governor

Xavier Becerra has been elected the next governor of California, the first Latino to win the state’s highest office.

In a race called by the AP on Tuesday night, Becerra, a Democrat, long was projected to easily defeat Republican Steve Hilton. Still, the win to replace term-limited Gavin Newsom comes on a deep blue night with Democrats taking control of the Senate and the House of Representatives and big scoring upsets in the governor’s office in Texas and Ohio.

Never leading in the Golden State, Hilton ran a campaign blasting California’s governance after years of Democratic dominance. At one widely derided point, the former Fox News host and adviser to ex-UK Prime Minister David Cameron, ran a sexually suggestive ad urging leftward voters to give him a try.

RELATED: Midterm Elections See Democrats Win House, Close In On Senate – Latest Watch on Deadline

But even though there has been no shortage of discontent within the state, there also is anti-Trump sentiment. The ex-Apprentice host endorsed Hilton in the primary, and the candidate struggled to distance himself from him. “This is not about who you hate in Washington,” he said in campaign appearances and ads.

RELATED: Newsom’s November Surprise: Boost CA Film & TV Tax Incentives To $1B ASAP, Says Exiting Governor

Becerra’s election marks a continuation of Democratic dominance, more than 20 years after a Republican was last elected governor. Becerra — the 68-year-old former California attorney general and Secretary of Health and Human Services under Joe Biden — ran a relatively low-key campaign, with just one debate with Hilton, and emphasized his experience as an asset in standing up to the Trump administration.

Becerra was considered an also-ran in the final few months before the June primary, but he emerged suddenly from a long list of contenders after the front-runner, Rep. Eric Swalwell (D-CA), dropped out amid sexual misconduct allegations.

At the CNN debate, both candidates were in agreement on the importance of addressing the flight of movie and TV production from the state. “If we give a tax credit, so long as we get more than $1 back for that dollar in tax credit, we’re going to do it because Hollywood belongs here,” Becerra said.

\RELATED: A Bizarre Finale For Midterms 2026: Haley Stevens Bombshell Created One Of The Cycle’s Memorable TV Moments

Hilton, though, blamed Democrats for the production flight. “My plan to bring Hollywood home would make us competitive with the best in the world and reduce the bureaucracy and the red tape, which also has been piled on by Xavier and his friends,” he said.

Becerra was well ahead in polls conducted in the state and perhaps got a further boost when Newsom on Monday proposed expanding the tax credit to $1 billion. Unlike Hilton and previous primary candidates, Becerra had ruled out uncapping the incentive — a position echoed by Newsom in his dramatic announcement this week. It should be noted, that surge in the currently $750 million-a-year film and TV tax credit program will now be the duty of Becerra to get passed and sign into law.

Newsom — always quick on the social media draw — posted congrats to Beceera on Tuesday night as “a product of the California dream who will stand up to Donald Trump.”

RELATED: Midterm Elections: Piers Morgan & Rashida Jones On How ‘Uncensored’s Going Into Uncharted Territory Tonight, The Trump Wild Card

Xavier Becerra will be a governor who will carry the torch for California — someone who, with Dr. Reyes, will represent our state and its diverse communities. A son immigrants, a product of the California dream who will stand up to Donald Trump and represent our values.…

Becerra will be the first Latino governor of California since Romualdo Pacheco in 1875. Unlike Becerra, Pacheco was not elected to the office but elevated to the post when the then sitting governor became a U.S. senator.

#3269. These 10 New Features Are Coming to iOS 27.3

Apple dropped the first developer beta for iOS 27.3 on Tuesday. While this update isn't as large as iOS 27 proper, it's surprisingly feature-filled for a 0.3 update. This is only a beta, so anything could (and likely will) change before Apple officially launches the update. But, as it stands, iOS 27.3 tests 10 new features—including one feature the company trialed in the previous beta.

Technically, anyone with a compatible iPhone can try out iOS 27.3 right now—assuming you enroll your Apple Account in the developer program. But a word of warning: Betas can be temperamental, and could be risky. As such, I'd recommend avoiding the beta until Apple releases the public beta, which comes after a bit more testing to iron out larger issues. Either way, make sure to make a full backup of your iPhone to a Mac or PC first, as issues with the beta could result in permanent data loss.

With watchOS 27, Apple released "Audio Intelligence," a new set of features for Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. Audio Intelligence uses the watches' new S11 chip, along with on-device AI and cloud-based AI, to run new features, like Sound Recognition and Shazam (music recognition).

With iOS 27.3, however, the company is now officially testing the other two Audio Intelligence features it originally announced with watchOS 27. First, there's Live Rewind: By double-clicking the watch crown, you can pull up a transcript of the last 15 seconds of a conversation. Siri Recap, on the other hand, displays summaries of conversations you had that day, in case you need a refresher on any chats you might have otherwise forgotten about,

The company generated some controversy when it first announced these two Audio Intelligence features, since, on the surface, it sounds like these new Apple Watches are essentially spying on people all day long. According to Apple, however, that isn't really the case. The company says Audio Intelligence is private, and never records or stores any audio. No speakers are ever identified, and text results (both transcripts and summaries) are deleted automatically after a set period of time unless the user saves them to the Siri app. You can read more about how Audio Intelligence works here.

Despite their claims, I'm sure there will still be strong feelings surrounding these Audio Intelligence features. We'll have to see whether Apple can prove Live Rewind and Siri Recap aren't all that creepy throughout the iOS 27.3 beta process.

iOS 27.3 also introduces app actions for Siri AI. Apple is testing new abilities for Siri AI, including organizing files, planning events, or adding photos to albums. You could ask Siri to organize your Downloads folder, or delete files that haven't been opened in more than a year. You could ask Siri to find a coffee shop you went to last week, or to save an article to your Reading List in Safari. You could ask Siri to check your calendar and set up a time for an event based on when you're free. You can even ask the assistant to schedule, edit, or unsend messages.

For example, you could ask Siri AI to help you plan a trip with your friends. You could ask the AI to put together a themed playlist in Apple Music, schedule a message to a group about an upcoming trip, organize the websites you've been visiting in Safari into a tab group, and, after the trip, ask Siri to move your best photos to your favorites album. These new actions work in the following apps: Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather. Developers can also add Siri AI app actions support to their own apps.

Apple started testing its new Health app with the iOS 27.2 beta, but pulled the redesign before the official release. Now, with iOS 27.3, the new app is back. The new Health app has a health dashboard for the first time, as well as new features like Health Age and movement assessments. It seems to be pulling from some popular competitor services, hopefully, for the better. For more on the new Health app, check out Lifehacker health editor Beth Skwarecki's explainer.

Continuing on the Health track, iOS 27.3 also introduces "Gym Strength." This is a new Fitness+ feature that offers a personalized four-week strength-training plan. You can customize these plans to meet your goals, experience level, and schedule, and they adapt as you progress. You'll get recommendations based on your experience with exercises, reps, and sets, including video demos for exercises. You can access Gym Strength on both iPhone and iPad, and Apple Watches are optional—though you can log your progress with the wearable if you have it.

Vertical tabs have been a favorite among browser aficionados, as they give you more screen real estate in your browser while keeping your tabs off the side. Apple hasn't made the jump—until now. This feature works with iPads running iPadOS 27.3 as well as Macs running macOS 27.3.

Another new Safari feature in testing is "Adaptive Dark Mode." This feature forces websites into a dark theme, if they don't have a native theme of their own. There are third-party apps that can do this, but this is the first time Apple has offered this feature built into Safari.

Apple is also testing new StandBy experiences with iOS 27.3, which were previously only available on the iPhone Duo. When you turn your iPhone sideways while plugged in, you'll find new Analog and Digital Clock faces with new customization options. There's also a new Photos face, with the option to pull images from Shared Albums.

"Reachability" pulls your iPhone's display down towards the bottom of the screen, so you can access items towards the top of the display with one hand. It's a useful feature for those of us with big iPhones, and now, there's no iPhone bigger than the Duo. With iOS 27.3, Apple is testing Reachability for its first foldable phone. It's a bit like the inverse of how Reachability currently works: You can swipe on the left or right side of your Duo's display to shift the other side of the screen towards your current position. If you're holding your Duo in your left hand, a swipe of the left side will pull the right side over to the left, and vice versa.

Apple is also rolling out new languages for Siri AI in iOS 27.3. Now, Apple's smart assistant supports Traditional Chinese, Vietnamese, Turkish, and Norwegian.

If you have an Apple Intelligence-compatible iPad running iPadOS 27.3, you now have access to Siri Mode in Camera. As with iOS, you can open the Camera app on iPadOS to access Siri Mode, and ask Siri about your surroundings.

#3268. iOS 27.3 and macOS 27.3 add Vertical Tabs, Adaptive Dark Mode, and more to Safari

Apple just released the first betas of iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, and macOS 27.3, with some big changes to Safari. The updates add a new vertical tab layout, Adaptive Dark Mode, and Siri AI Custom Actions.

Safari in iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, and macOS 27.3 is adding a new Vertical Tabs design option. If you choose this design, you’ll see your tabs arranged vertically along the left-hand side of Safari rather than along the top, as in the traditional Safari design.

By default, Vertical Tabs show as icons in order to maximize vertical and horizontal space. If you’d like, you can also resize the tab bar to see website titles.

To try Vertical Tabs in the new iOS 27.3 beta, head to the Settings app, choose Apps, tap Safari, then look for the new Vertical Tabs option. On Mac and iPad, the feature can also be enabled via the “View” menu in the Safari app directly.

Vertical tab layouts have become an increasingly popular web browser feature. Arc from The Browser Company popularized the option. Arc, however, ceased development last year, and The Browser Company announced last month that it will discontinue it altogether in December.

If you regularly visit a website that doesn’t support Dark Mode, Apple’s next round of software updates adds Adaptive Dark Mode. This will automatically apply Dark Mode to websites that don’t support the feature.

If Dark Mode is enabled on your iPhone, iPad, or Mac and you visit a website that doesn’t support it, you’ll see a new “Try” button. If you tap this, Safari will automatically create a Dark Mode version of the website.

You can choose to have Adaptive Dark Mode automatically kick in or use it on a site-by-site basis.

I’ve been using Noir for Dark Mode in Safari, I am very curious to see how it compares against Adaptive Dark Mode.

Finally, Siri AI can now take direct action on tabs in iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, and macOS 27.3. This includes things like using Siri to move, sort, organize, and close your tabs.

In a future update, Siri’s on-screen awareness will also expand to include the entire content of a website, not just what’s visible on the screen at a particular moment.

iOS 27.3, macOS 27.3, and iPadOS 27.3 are rolling out to developers for beta testing today. The update will likely be released to everyone sometime in December. What do you think of these new Safari features? Will you try out the new Vertical Tabs feature? Let us know down in the comments.

There’s always something new to watch on Netflix, but with a new month comes plenty of fresh additions, meaning the top 10 list can change up pretty quickly. With so many titles competing for your attention, deciding what deserves a spot on your watchlist can be tricky. That’s where I come in. Netflix’s top 10 is a good starting point, but not every trending series is necessarily worth your time. So, I’ve picked out three shows from this week’s most popular picks that I think deserve a look.

This week’s selection covers everything from an intimate documentary about the life, career and struggles of a much-loved sitcom star to the third season of a seriously charming romantic comedy. There’s also a gripping supernatural mystery about a seemingly ordinary town that traps anyone who enters, with its residents desperately searching for a way home. Whether you’re after real-life stories, a bit of romance or some seriously unsettling mysteries, there’s something here to keep you entertained.

Note: This list is based on the Netflix U.S. top 10 shows as of Tuesday, November 3, 2026.

“The One About Matthew Perry” is a three-part documentary that explores the life, career and tragic death of the beloved “Friends” star. Released just ahead of the three-year anniversary of his passing, the documentary was developed with input from people who knew Perry before and after his period of peak sitcom fame. It also takes inspiration from the classic “Friends” episode titles, choosing to steer clear of sensationalized Hollywood gossip and instead offers something raw and honest.

Through never-before-heard testimonies from his sister, lifelong friends and former colleagues, alongside previously unreleased family photographs and videos, the series looks back at Perry’s journey from aspiring actor to Hollywood favorite as Chandler Bing. It also takes a look at his long-running battle with addiction, repeated attempts at recovery and the advocacy work he became passionate about. From his rise to fame to his final days, it’s an intimate portrait of the man behind one of television’s most recognizable characters.

Stream "The One About Matthew Perry" on Netflix

Fancy a cozy romantic comedy to binge this week? Netflix’s “Nobody Wants This” is a great place to start, with all three seasons available to catch up on. Created by Erin Foster and loosely inspired by her own experience meeting her husband, the series brings a fresh, grown-up take on the rom-com. I especially love its mix of genuinely funny (and awkward) moments and more honest relationship drama, making it an easy watch if you’re after something funny, charming and a little bit heartfelt. Plus, the two leads have some sizzling chemistry.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

“Nobody Wants This” centers around Joanne (Kristen Bell), an outspoken podcast host who meets Noah (Adam Brody), a recently single rabbi, at a dinner party. Despite their very different backgrounds, the pair quickly hit it off and decide to see where things go. However, their new relationship soon brings them into each other’s complicated family lives, with Joanne’s sister Morgan (Justine Lupe) and Noah’s brother Sasha (Timothy Simons) never too far from the action. This Netflix comedy follows the couple as they figure out what building a future together might actually look like.

I couldn't be happier to see “From” land on Netflix, as it’s genuinely one of my favorite shows and deserves to reach a much bigger audience. It’s already great to see it making its way onto the platform’s trending list, and I'm hoping it climbs even higher over the next few days. For anyone who hasn’t watched it yet, this is one of the best mystery-box horror shows around, packed with bizarre twists and many questions. With season 5 set to bring the story to a close, I’m glad the creators have a clear endpoint in sight. Hopefully, that means we finally get the answers we’ve been waiting for.

“From” is set in a mysterious small town that traps everyone who enters, leaving its residents desperately searching for a way home. When the Matthews family takes a wrong turn during a road trip, they find themselves stuck alongside a group of strangers who have been trying to escape for years. Led by Sheriff Boyd Stevens (Harold Perrineau), the residents must find ways to survive, particularly after dark, when terrifying human-like creatures emerge from the surrounding forest. As new arrivals bring fresh questions, finding a way out proves harder than anyone imagined.

#3265. Midterm Elections: Democrats Win Control Of U.S. Senate; Maine And Michigan Races Still Not Yet Called

Democrats will control the Senate and the House in the next Congress, regaining both chambers in what will be a consequential rebuke and check on Donald Trump.

The AP projected that the party would take control, shortly after major network calls.

Democrats already have flipped seats in Texas, South Carolina, North Carolina, Kansas, Iowa and Ohio. Races in Alaska and Maine are still outstanding, and it was still unclear if they would hold seats in Michigan and Minnesota.

In a short interview with the NYT, Trump promised to be absolutely willing to accept those results “of the midterms.” Spreading responsibility for the GOP defeats on others like soon to be ex-Texas governor Greg Abbott, Trump added, “We’ll work with the Democrats, and we’ll, you know, look forward to working with them.” He also spoke to CBS News, telling Weijia Jiang, “Congratulations to the Democrats, and I look forward to working with you for the good of our country.” Watch on Deadline

Trump also posted on Truth Social, “I’m going to become a Political Pundit, both good and bad, on the reasons these Candidates won and lost!” And he complained again about Fox News featuring Bill de Blasio’s analysis. “FoxNews bears responsibility for these losses by constantly and consistently putting on the Dumocrat opposition, and worse,” he wrote.

With Dems taking the House and the Senate, he’ll have to. Or as Brett Baier just said on Fox News, “Democrats sealed the deal.”

Democratic control of the Senate will have a huge impact on oversight and investigations, but potentially on the Supreme Court if there are one or more vacancies. If so, Democrats could refuse to consider confirmation, as Republicans did when Barack Obama nominated Merrick Garland in 2016.

Democrats Get Closer To Flipping Senate With Adam Hamilton’s Victory In Kansas, 8:32 p.m. PT/11:32 p.m. ET: Adam Hamilton will become the first Democrat to win a U.S. Senate seat in Kansas since 1932, scoring another blue wave upset by defeating incumbent Republican Roger Marshall.

The AP called the race for Hamilton at around 8:25 p.m. PT/11:25 p.m. PT.

Hamilton, a Methodist minister, ran a centrist campaign in the reliably red state. Democrats already have flipped seats in North Carolina, Texas and Ohio.

Texas Stunner As James Talarico Wins U.S. Senate Seat And Gina Hinojosa Wins Governor Race, 7:59 p.m. : James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa scored major upsets in Texas, winning the U.S. Senate seat and the state governor’s race, respectively, in a state that has not elected a statewide Democrat in almost three decades.

The AP called the race for both candidates in the 8 p.m. PT/11 p.m. ET hour, following news networks.

Talarico defeated Ken Paxton, the state’s attorney general, who faced a series of scandals that turned off independents and some Republicans.

Hinojosa defeated Republican Greg Abbott, who has been governor since 2015.Talarico was a favorite of Hollywood donors, who warmed to the possibility of flipping the seat as the year went on and his polling improved. With personal charisma in which he talked about his faith, Talarico proved to belie the image of a candidate of the far left. And Talarico embraced Trump’s nickname for him, “Talafreako,” in a dose of campaign irony.

“This is history,” Erin Burnett said on CNN, reporting from Talarico’s victory party.

Talarico earned words of praise last year from Joe Rogan, a sign that he had crossover appeal even to those who voted for Trump in 2024. That helped propel his Senate race.

His victory also is a rebuke of Elon Musk, who poured $168 million into the Senate Leadership Fund, with much of it going to support Ken Paxton, per The New York Times.As surprising as Talarico and Hinojosa’s victory was, it was not the only surprise of the evening. That was Democrat Annie Andrews’ win in South Carolina, defeating Trump’s choice of Darline Graham, appointed to the seat after the death of her brother, longtime Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-SC). “This is an earthquake in politics,” NBC News’ Savannah Guthrie said. Democrats also have flipped U.S. Senate seats in North Carolina, where Roy Cooper won, and in Ohio, where Sherrod Brown has won.

Even before major networks called the race for Talarico, the senator he replaced, John Cornyn, offered congratulations. He wrote on X, “The voters have spoken, and I want to extend my congratulations to James Talarico on his election to the U.S. Senate. I look forward to meeting him and offering my assistance with his transition as he prepares to serve Texans in the U.S. Senate.”

Democrats To Take Control Of The House Of Representatives, Flip South Carolina Senate Seat, 7:09 p.m. PT/10:09 p.m. ET: Democrats were projected to win control of the House of Representatives, giving a check on Donald Trump for the remaining two years of his term.

As Trump briskly started blaming everyone but himself, NewsNation was the first to project House control, followed by MS NOW and CNN.

Avoiding the fact that midterms are almost always a referendum on the incumbent in the White Hoouse Trump wrote: “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!”

As the House now in ruled by Speaker in waiting Hakeen Jefferies and Trump’s pledge of $5,000 to every American if the GOP won, the Senate is looking pretty blue too.

On MS NOW, Rachel Maddow said, “In the second Donald Trump presidential term, the Democratic Party and America’s voters have defied the first of those dynamics in seizing back power for the opposition party in Congress, and now we will see if they can defy that second dynamic as well, whether they can use the full power of the legislative branch, whether they can take up all the space the founders intended when they wrote the powers of Congress as Article One of the United States Constitution, and we will see whether this president reacts to this election and this massive loss like a lame duck or like a wounded bull.”

Rep. Robert Garcia (D-CA), in line to chair the House Oversight Committee, posted on X, ‘LAWYER UP.” He has already talked of multiple investigations, including of corporate donors to Trump’s White House ballroom.

In a particularly harsh rejection of Trump, Democrat Dr Annie Andrews had emerged victorious in the South Carolina Senate race against appointed Sen. Darline Graham (R-SC).

Earlier in the night, as results had Andrews moving ahead, MS Now’s Jen Psaki proclaimed “Holy cow, what a moment there, because that was not even a race a couple of weeks ago.” After the race was called for Dr. Andrews, Fox News’ Dana Perino lamented “there are some races that are going to be too hard to overcome.” The former Bush press secretary and The Five co-host admitted she didn’t think the sister of the late Lindsey Graham would be one of those races.

RELATED: The Key 2026 Midterm Races Hollywood Is Watching

As they have all night as the blue wins have piled up, the FNC hosts blamed the war with Iran as the cause of the GOP and MAGA losses.

“It’s sad to me,” decried Sean Hannity of the Dems flip of the SC seat and the sibling Graham’s defeat. it could get very sad for Trump pal Hannity as the Dems are looking closer and closer to snagging the Senate. Over on CNN, conservative Scott Jennings, who is being sued by Hasan Piker for alleged defamation, told his fellow panelists “the wheels of democracy” turned on the elites tonight. A self-declared shocked Jake Tapper just let out a “someone throw a blanket on me” over Andrews win.

Out on the West Coast, outgoing Golden State governor and anticipated 2028 POTUS contender Gavin Newsom added Andrews to fellow Dems he was congratulating as a party leader. In full Trump caps, Newsom tweeted: “THIS IS HUGE FOR SOUTH CAROLINA AND THE NATION”

CONGRATS @ANNIEANDREWSMD!! THIS IS HUGE FOR SOUTH CAROLINA AND THE NATION. https://t.co/V2ABGjZDqT

Another potential big blue win Tuesday happened in Trump territory of Ohio with Dem Amy Acton beating 2024 POTUS candidate Vivek Ramaswamy.

In a homage to Megyn Kelly’s famous live stroll down the hall to the Fox Decision Desk on Election Night 2020 to confirm a state win by Joe Biden, Anderson Cooper took viewers through the catacombs of CNN tonight to get the skinny on where the 2026 midterms stand and where it could go.

Pundits Start To Call It a Blue Wave, 6:18 PM PT: “It’s everywhere,” CNN’s John King said shortly before 6 p.m. PT/9 p.m. PT of the shift toward Democrats so far shaping up during the evening.

Even in states like Florida, where Republican Ashley Moody was expected to win the Senate race and Republican Byron Donalds was projected to win the governor’s race, the margins were closer than expected.

“This night is shaping up to be a blue tsunami,” CNN’s Kasie Hunt said, saying that it was the “greatest fear for Republicans that Democrats didn’t dare hope for.”

In Texas, James Talarico was leading in the race for U.S. Senate and Gina Hinojosa was leading in the race for governor in that state. Adam Hamilton was leading in Kansas, hoping to become the first Democrat elected to the Senate from the state since 1932. Democrat Annie Andrews was leading in deep red South Carolina.

Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms was projected to win the governorship in Georgia, flipping the statehouse. History is also made as she is the first Black woman elected governor in the United States.

On MS NOW, Symone Townsend Sanders said, “Today, America has elected its first Black woman as governor in this country. Keisha Lance Bottoms made history tonight, but she didn’t run on making history. She ran on the issues, and I think that resonated with folks in the state.”

She added, “Whatever else happens tonight, this is a reminder that in America the people have the power. And Georgia has a governor named Keisha.”

On NBC News, anchor Tom Llamas said that what was happening was more than traditional midterms which favor the party out of power but a “shift,” citing the candidates.

On Fox News, Peter Doocy reported that there was a reception in the East Room and that some staffers have ordered from the Cheesecake Factory. That was a reference to Barack Obama’s joke at a rally last week over Donald Trump’s choice for White House decor.

“I think Trump’s hurdle is the Iran conflict, high gas prices, high food prices,” Fox News’ Laura Ingraham said. “That’s really it and Trump decided – and I asked him this in an interview the last time I interviewed him, if you lose your entire majority, as a result of what looks like, you know, high prices, will the Iran conflict, as far as gas, be worth it? He said ‘I wouldn’t change a thing.”

Jon Ossoff Projected To Win Georgia, 4:56 p.m. PT/7:56 p.m. ET: Networks made their first major race projection: Jon Ossoff, winning reelection to another U.S. Senate term in Georgia.

NBC News made the call in the 4 p.m. PT/7 p.m. ET hour, and was followed by CBS News and CNN. AP called the race around 5 p.m. PT/8 p.m. ET.

His victory is not a surprise, given his position in the polls, but Ossoff had been a key target for Republicans at the start of the midterm.

Already, Ossoff has been mentioned as a 2028 presidential prospect, even though he has denied that he is interested. His race also was among the closely watched by entertainment industry Democrats, as he had trekked to Los Angeles multiple times on fundraising swings.

Speaking to John King minutes before the 5 p.m. PT/8 p.m. ET poll closing on much of the East Coast and just after CNN called the Georgia Senate race for Ossoff, Jake Tapper noted the outlet has “a cautious desk.” Certainly tonight, with lawyers from the DOJ and lawyers from the Democratic Party fanning out all over the nation in anticipated of contested races, almost all outlets online and on TV are playing it cool to not ignite any friction.

Over on NewsNation, anchor Blake Burman captured that mood when he said of early data: “Here’s what they are projecting at this point in time, and I use that word projecting, in the House. A very strong night, potentially, for Democrats.”

Over on Fox, former Trump press secretary Karoline Leavitt gave her ex-boss a poised dose of reality with some qualification. “The reality of the night …is that history is not on his side,” Leavitt said of “pragmatic” Trump, who has been hate-watching Fox tonight. Adding to Levitt’s election desk debut, Jesse Watters was blunt: “It’s not a red wave, I don’t think we’re going to get our $5,000 checks.”

Another call also came shortly after the 5 p.m. PT/8 p.m. ET, with Josh Shapiro projected to win reelection to governor of Pennsylvania and J.B. Pritzker to governor of Illinois. Both victories are not surprises. On the other side of the aisle, Republican Ashley Moody, appointed to the U.S. Senate last year, was projected to win in Florida.

Donald Trump Rages Fox News For Platforming Jessica Tarlov And Democrats, 3:50 p.m. PT/6:50 p.m. ET: Donald Trump has been watching The Five on the early part of Election Night, and once again raged at its sole Democratic co-host, Jessica Tarlov.

He wrote on Truth Social, “Watching the Pre-Election Results on FoxNews, but I can’t stand Jessica Tarlov’s voice — DUMB AS A ROCK, but it’s the voice that gets me. Have to go somewhere else until that LOSER is off the air — I’ll be back later! President DONALD J. TRUMP”

He even texted one of the show’s other co-hosts, Greg Gutfeld, who read it on air. “Greg, tell Tarlov, who is the WORST, gas prices are lower than they were for Biden and Obama and they allowed Iran to have a nuclear bomb. Furthermore, I inherited the worst crisis inflation in history from Sleepy Joe. Prices are heading DOWN. Just like all other prices, and so is inflation, which is 1.7% the last three months. And there will be no ‘Nuclear bomb.'”

The co-hosts then laughed and riffed a bit.

In the 6 p.m. ET/3 p.m. PT hour, Trump posted again about Fox News, this time to complain about their voter poll results.

He wrote, “The FoxNews Poll, always the worst, is so insulting with the questions they ask. Every question is a hit job, and every answer is ‘BULLSHIT!’ This has been going on for years. President DONALD J. TRUMP” He also posted, “No wonder FoxNews Ratings are collapsing, and they’re going to go down a lot further. They’re way down, not because of me, but because they are AGAINST me!”

Fox News does its own polling during the campaign, but the data shown on election night is The Voter Poll, the SSRS consortium of all the major networks who get the same data.

Tarlov later posted on X, “I realize my comments highlighting the highest gas prices on any Election Day aggravated the president, but reality is a tricky thing and he should get better at dealing with it.”

Later, Trump spoke to CBS News’ Robert Costa, and the president vowed the use the “tremendous powers” of the presidency if Democrats gain control of Congress. That means executive orders and vetoes. “We won the Slaughter case and the Slaughter case gives the president tremendous powers that it never had before,” he told Costa, referring to the Supreme Court decision that affirmed his power to remove a member of the Federal Trade Commission.

Networks Comb Through First Voter Poll Data Showing Dismal Numbers For Trump, 2:28 p.m. PT: Networks got their first glimpse at the sentiment of the electorate, with a batch of preliminary voter poll information showing dismal approval ratings for Donald Trump and the state of the country.

Per CNN, Trump’s approval rating was at 38% with 62% disapproving. That is seven points lower than Trump’s approval in the midterm of 2018.

The top issue for voters was the economy, at 39%, followed by democracy at 32%.

On another question, 44% of voters said that their financial situation was worse than two years ago, 18% said it was better and 38% said that things were about the same.

Some 37% of voters said that they were dissatisfied with the state of things in the country, and 38% said that they were downright angry. About 25% said they were enthusiastic or satisifed.

“That is an electorate that is hungry for change,” said CNN’s David Chalian, who cautioned that the numbers will shift as the day goes on.

That said, Jake Tapper noted that the 44% of voters saying they were worse off was below some of the recent polling on a similar question, although that may be just a small bright spot for Trump and Republicans.

Other polls showed that 65% thought that Trump has worsened economic conditions, 28% thought he had improved conditions and 8% thought he had no impact. Some 61% thought that he has prioritized his personal interests, and 39% thought he had put at the forefront the country’s interests.

CNN debuted a new set, with its team and different stations around a giant studio, and a roving camera keying in on them for analysis. Kaitlan Collins, CNN’s chief White House correspondent, reported that the mood is “fatalistic” in the White House, while his allies say he Trump has been “in denial” about gas prices. “The question still is how he takes it and how he responds to it,” she said.

The data, known as The Voter Poll, is from early, vote-by-mail and election day voters and is conducted by SSRS, with all the major networks subscribing. While the numbers will change, they can offer a hint of what will happen later in the evening. Early in the evening in 2024, when Chris Wallace was still at CNN, he doubted that Kamala Harris could win with such a high “country on wrong track” figure.

MS NOW, in its first major election night coverage since the split from Comcast, keyed in on one figure: 54% said that corruption was crucial in their vote, and 46% said it was not crucial. Filmmaker Ken Burns was a guest, telling Nicolle Wallace that “one of the big disappointments, in addition to Article One, the legislative, is of course the way in which the Supreme Court has turned and become sort of an instrumentality of the executive, which was not what was intended at all.”

Fox News featured The Five, the top show on cable news, and ran the Voter Poll information on a side screen.

The midterms will be a test for legacy media, not just as they deploy new technology, but because of the flood of polling that generally showed Democrats were in for a possible “wave” election, with rising odds to take the House and the Senate.

But a number of pollsters have been cautious about addressing the potential for a polling error, particularly the difficulty of reaching right-leaning voters in rural areas. Trump has often dismissed his bad polls as “fake,” but the issue of polling reliability came to the fore when his FCC chairman, Brendan Carr, warned broadcasters about amplifying fraudulent surveys. Although his statement came after the revelation that two polls cited by prognosticators were made up, he remark drew pushback from Democrats and others that he was trying to chill election coverage.

The evening is the biggest night of the year for the linear networks, a chance for them to put forth their star anchors and personalities. But this cycle they face substantial competition for eyeballs from a wave of influencers and content creators, even news stars formerly in their ranks. They include Jim Acosta and Katie Couric, teamed for a live stream as results come in, and Chris Cillizza and Chuck Todd, who will have their own coverage in a partnership with Decision Desk HQ.

Legacy networks have been trying to keep viewers within their universe. NBC News, for example, is planning 13 hours of coverage on the broadcast network, along with a stream of its data expert, Steve Kornacki.

Will it be a blue wave? That will be a prevailing question throughout the evening’s coverage, starting with the first poll closings at 6 p.m. ET/3 p.m. PT in the eastern part of Kentucky and Indiana. The rest in the states close at 7 p.m. ET/4 p.m. ET, as do Georgia, South Carolina, Vermont and Virginia.

#3264. watchOS 27.3 beta adds new Siri Recap and Live Rewind features for Apple Watch

Apple has released the first beta of watchOS 27.3 for developers, including two new Audio Intelligence features for Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4: Siri Recap and Live Rewind.

Apple first announced these features at its special event in September, saying they would “arrive in beta later this year.”

As a refresher, Siri Recap creates high-level summaries of conversations that you can review later. When the feature is enabled, Apple Intelligence will automatically generate a title and key points that you can review in the Siri app on iPhone.

Siri Recap ambiently takes notes on your conversations throughout your day and creates high-level Apple Intelligence–generated summaries that you can use later to jog your memory, so you can stay present in the moment. Your summaries auto-delete after 7 days if you choose not to save them.

You can turn on Siri Recap in the Watch app on iPhone. When you enable it, you can set a schedule based on time and/or location, or you can manually turn it on or off. You can also access it via Control Center on Apple Watch.

Live Rewind, meanwhile, helps you recall what was just said in a conversation. You can activate Live Rewind by double-pressing the Digital Crown, and then see a transcript of the previous 15 seconds of a conversation.

Live Rewind recalls what was just said in the last 15 seconds by showing a text snippet on your Apple Watch when you double-press the Digital Crown, so you can catch something you missed or are less familiar with. You can ask Siri about the content of the snippet or simply save it to the Siri app.

Siri Recap’s summary is described as a “brief, high-level summary of conversations,” not a transcript. Apple says it will “exclude sensitive information like financial information or government-assigned identifiers.”

Live Rewind text snippets and Siri Recap summaries are end-to-end encrypted. Apple says the features “do not create or store audio recordings, and raw audio used for processing is completely inaccessible to the operating systems, apps, the user, or Apple.” The company uses the S11 chip’s Secure Exclave to power the features, a “dedicated hardware-isolated compartment that processes audio in complete isolation from the rest of the system, then immediately deletes it.”

Siri Recap and Live Rewind are available in beta with watchOS 27.3, which is available now for developers.
